title: 04. Caching: Distributed Cache
summary: A distributed cache is a cache that spans multiple nodes, partitioning the key space across them (typically via consistent hashing) so the cluster's total capacity and throughput scale horizontally, and replicating each…
objectives: What is a distributed cache, and when do you need one (vs a single-node cache)?
What is consistent hashing, and why is it used for partitioning?
How does Redis Cluster's hash slot mechanism differ from generic consistent hashing?
What is async replication, and why do most distributed caches use it instead of sync?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A distributed cache is a **cache that spans multiple nodes**, partitioning the key space across them (typically via consistent hashing) so the cluster's total capacity and throughput scale horizontally, and replicating each partition to one or more replicas for high availability — exemplified by Redis Cluster, Memcached, Netflix's EVCache, and Twitter's Redis clusters, all of which trade the simplicity of a single-node cache for the operational complexity of sharding, replication, failover, and cross-node consistency.

A single-node cache has hard limits: a single Redis instance caps at the RAM of one machine (typically 256GB–1TB), a single CPU core for command processing (~100k QPS), and a single network interface (~10–25 Gbps). When the working set exceeds RAM or the QPS exceeds a single node's capacity, the cache must be distributed across multiple nodes. The fundamental design questions are: how to partition the key space across nodes (so each node handles a fraction of the load), how to replicate each partition (so a node failure doesn't lose data), how to route requests to the right node (so clients find their keys), and how to handle node failures (so the cluster stays available). Each question has well-established answers, but the combination determines the cache's characteristics: capacity (sum of node RAM), throughput (sum of node QPS), availability (function of replication factor and failover speed), and consistency (function of replication strategy — sync vs async).

The **partitioning** strategy is the foundation, and consistent hashing is the dominant answer. The naive approach — `hash(key) % N` — assigns each key to one of N nodes, but adding or removing a node (N changes) reassigns almost every key, causing a massive cache miss storm. Consistent hashing fixes this by placing both nodes and keys on a ring (hash space): each key is assigned to the next node clockwise on the ring. When a node is added or removed, only the keys in that node's segment of the ring move — typically `1/N` of the keys, not all of them. This makes cluster resizing cheap: adding a node to a 10-node cluster moves ~10% of keys (vs ~100% with modulo hashing). To balance load, each physical node is placed on the ring multiple times via "virtual nodes" (vnodes) — typically 100–200 vnodes per physical node, which spreads the keys evenly and prevents hot spots from ring-position clustering. Real-world: Dynamo (Amazon's KV store) popularized consistent hashing with vnodes; Cassandra uses it (default 256 vnodes); Redis Cluster uses a variant (hash slots, 16384 slots distributed across nodes); Memcached's clients (libketama) use consistent hashing with vnodes. The trade-off: consistent hashing adds ~1 hop of routing (the client must compute the ring position and find the owning node) but makes resizing cheap.

The **replication** strategy determines availability and durability. Each partition (key range) is replicated to R nodes (the replication factor); writes go to the primary and propagate to the replicas. The two strategies: (1) **Sync replication** — the primary waits for all (or a quorum of) replicas to acknowledge before returning success to the client. Strong consistency (a read from any replica returns the latest write), but higher write latency (waits for the slowest replica) and reduced availability (if a replica is down, writes fail unless the quorum is met). (2) **Async replication** — the primary returns success after writing locally, and replicas catch up asynchronously. Lower write latency and higher availability (a replica being down doesn't block writes), but eventual consistency (a read from a lagging replica may return stale data). Most distributed caches use async replication for the latency/availability win, accepting eventual consistency (caches are not the source of truth — the DB is — so brief inconsistency is tolerable). Real-world: Redis Cluster uses async replication (a primary failure can lose the last few unreplicated writes, but the cache repopulates from the DB on miss); Cassandra uses tunable consistency (per-query sync or async); Netflix's EVCache uses async multi-region replication. The replication factor is typically 2–3 (one primary + 1–2 replicas) — enough to survive a node failure without data loss, but not so high that write amplification is excessive.

The **routing** strategy determines how clients find the owning node. Three patterns: (1) **Client-side routing** — the client has a copy of the cluster topology (the ring) and routes directly to the owning node. Lowest latency (no proxy hop) but the client must be cluster-aware and must update its topology when the cluster changes. Redis Cluster, Memcached (with libketama), and Cassandra use this. (2) **Proxy routing** — the client sends to a proxy (Twemproxy, Redis Cluster proxy, Mcrouter), which routes to the owning node. Simple clients (no cluster awareness) but adds a hop (latency) and a bottleneck (the proxy). (3) **Coordinator routing** — the client sends to any node, which acts as a coordinator and forwards to the owning node. Used by Dynamo-style systems. The dominant pattern for caches is client-side routing (Redis Cluster, Memcached) because latency is critical and the client library can handle topology updates. Real-world: Redis Cluster's clients (redis-py-cluster, Jedis, lettcue) maintain a slot-to-node map and update it via cluster gossip; Memcached's clients (libketama, spymemcached) maintain a ring of vnodes; Twitter's Twemproxy was a proxy that handled routing for both Redis and Memcached but has been largely replaced by client-side routing.

The **failover** strategy determines what happens when a node dies. The cluster must detect the failure (via gossip or heartbeats), promote a replica to primary (for the partitions the dead node owned), and update the routing table so clients send to the new primary. Redis Cluster uses a quorum-based failover: nodes gossip about each other, and if a majority of masters agree a node is down, they promote its replica. The failover takes 10–30 seconds (detection + replica promotion + client topology update), during which the partitions owned by the dead node are unavailable (writes fail, reads fail unless the client falls back to a replica). Netflix's EVCache uses a different approach: all replicas are equal (no primary), and clients write to all replicas in parallel (read from any); a node failure just means one fewer replica, with no failover needed. Real-world: Redis Cluster's failover is documented in its specification; Netflix's EVCache is designed for multi-region HA with no primary/replica distinction; Memcached has no built-in failover (clients must handle it by rehashing or using a proxy). The trade-off: faster failover reduces downtime but risks split-brain (two nodes think they're the primary); slower failover is safer but extends the outage.

The **hot key problem** is thedistributed cache's throughput bottleneck. Even with perfect partitioning, a single key accessed at 100k QPS overwhelms its owning node (which has ~100k QPS capacity). The key is "hot" — it's a single partition that's saturated while other partitions are idle. Mitigations: (1) **Read replicas** — replicate the hot key to multiple nodes and have clients read from any replica (load-balanced). This scales reads but not writes (writes still go to the primary). (2) **Key splitting** — replace `hot_key` with `hot_key:0`, `hot_key:1`, ..., `hot_key:9` (10 copies), and have clients pick one at random. This scales both reads and writes (each copy is on a different node), but the application must keep the copies in sync (write to all, or use a write-through pattern). (3) **Local caching** — add an in-process cache (Caffeine) in front of the distributed cache for hot keys, so most reads don't hit the distributed cache at all. Real-world: Twitter's cache for trending topics uses key splitting (each trend is replicated to multiple nodes); Netflix's EVCache uses local caching for the top 1000 popular titles; Redis Cluster documents the hot-key problem and recommends read replicas + client-side load balancing.

The **multi-region** distributed cache is the most complex variant. A global app (users in US, EU, Asia) needs caches in each region for low-latency reads, but the caches must stay consistent across regions. The strategies: (1) **Independent regional caches with cross-region invalidation** — each region has its own cache, and writes invalidate the other regions' caches via a global pub/sub (covered in Topic 10). Eventual consistency (typically 1–5s lag), but each region's reads are local (low latency). (2) **Global cache with regional read replicas** — a single primary (in one region) with read replicas in each region. Reads are local (from the replica), but writes go to the primary (cross-region latency, typically 50–200ms). (3) **Multi-master** — each region's cache is a primary, and writes are replicated bidirectionally. Lowest write latency but the hardest to keep consistent (conflict resolution). Most apps use (1) — independent regional caches with cross-region invalidation — because it's the simplest to reason about and the consistency lag (1–5s) is acceptable for most data. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache is multi-region with async replication; Cloudflare's cache is per-POP with global purge; Discord uses per-region Redis with cross-region pub/sub invalidation.

The **operational concerns** of a distributed cache are substantial: monitoring (per-node memory, CPU, QPS, eviction rate, replication lag), capacity planning (when to add nodes, how to rebalance), backup and restore (RDB snapshots, AOF for Redis; no built-in backup for Memcached), security (TLS, ACLs), and deployment (rolling restarts, version upgrades). Redis Cluster's `CLUSTER INFO` and `CLUSTER NODES` commands expose the cluster state; Prometheus + Grafana dashboards are standard for monitoring. The decision to use a distributed cache (vs a single node or no cache) should consider these operational costs — a single Redis instance is much simpler to run than a 10-node Redis Cluster, and for many apps the single instance is sufficient. Real-world: small-to-medium apps use a single Redis (with a replica for HA); large apps (Twitter, Netflix, Discord) use distributed caches with dedicated cache teams.

Each node owns a segment of the ring (multiple segments via vnodes for balance). The key is assigned to the next node clockwise on the ring. Adding or removing a node moves only ~1/N of the keys. 2. **Async replication for HA**: Each primary's data is replicated asynchronously to one or more replicas. Writes return success after the primary writes locally (low latency), and replicas catch up via the replication stream. A replica lag of milliseconds is typical. 3. **Client-side routing**: The client maintains a slot-to-node map (updated via cluster gossip) and routes directly to the owning primary (1 hop, low latency). On a moved key, the server responds with a MOVED redirect and the client updates its map. 4. **Failover**: When a primary dies, gossip detects the failure (5–15s), a majority of masters mark it FAIL, and the replica is promoted to primary (1–2s). The cluster broadcasts the new topology, and clients update their routing. Total downtime: ~10–30s for the dead node's slots.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Consistent hash ring with virtual nodes for balance.
- A distributed cache with: - Consistent hashing for partitioning (1 primary per key). - Async replication to R replicas (sequential on ring). -…
- Return [primary, replica1, replica2, ...] for this key.
- Promote the next replica for all keys owned by the dead node.
- Distributed cache with consistent hashing + replication.
- Demonstrates: ring with vnodes, key routing, async replication,
- Failover (replica promotion), and hotspot detection.
- Single cache node (in-process simulation)

**Defines:** `_hash()`, `CacheNode`, `HashRing`, `DistributedCache`

```python
# Distributed cache with consistent hashing + replication.
# Demonstrates: ring with vnodes, key routing, async replication,
# failover (replica promotion), and hotspot detection.

import bisect
import hashlib
import random
import threading
import time
from typing import Any, Optional

def _hash(s: str) -> int:
    return int(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)

# ---------- Single cache node (in-process simulation) ---------- #
class CacheNode:
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self._data: dict = {}
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self.is_alive = True
        self.is_primary = True
        self.primary_of: Optional[str] = None  # if replica, who's the primary
        self.stats = {"reads": 0, "writes": 0, "replications": 0}

    def get(self, key: str) -> Optional[Any]:
        if not self.is_alive:
            return None
        with self._lock:
            self.stats["reads"] += 1
            return self._data.get(key)

    def set(self, key: str, value: Any) -> None:
        if not self.is_alive:
            return
        with self._lock:
            self._data[key] = value
            self.stats["writes"] += 1

    def replicate(self, key: str, value: Any) -> None:
        if not self.is_alive:
            return
        with self._lock:
            self._data[key] = value
            self.stats["replications"] += 1

    def kill(self) -> None:
        self.is_alive = False

    def revive(self) -> None:
        self.is_alive = True

# ---------- Consistent hash ring with vnodes ---------- #
class HashRing:
    """Consistent hash ring with virtual nodes for balance.

    Each physical node is placed on the ring `vnodes` times,
    spreading keys evenly and minimizing movement on add/remove.
    """

    def __init__(self, vnodes: int = 100):
        self.vnodes = vnodes
        self._ring: list = []           # sorted list of (hash, node_name)
        self._nodes: dict = {}          # node_name -> CacheNode

    def add_node(self, node: CacheNode) -> None:
        self._nodes[node.name] = node
        for i in range(self.vnodes):
            h = _hash(f"{node.name}#{i}")
            bisect.insort(self._ring, (h, node.name))

    def remove_node(self, name: str) -> None:
        self._ring = [(h, n) for (h, n) in self._ring if n != name]
        del self._nodes[name]

    def get_node(self, key: str) -> Optional[CacheNode]:
        if not self._ring:
            return None
        h = _hash(key)
        idx = bisect.bisect_right(self._ring, (h, "")) % len(self._ring)
        return self._nodes[self._ring[idx][1]]

    def get_node_name(self, key: str) -> Optional[str]:
        node = self.get_node(key)
        return node.name if node else None

# ---------- Distributed cache with replication + failover ---------- #
class DistributedCache:
    """A distributed cache with:
    - Consistent hashing for partitioning (1 primary per key).
    - Async replication to R replicas (sequential on ring).
    - Failover: if primary dies, promote next replica.
    """

    def __init__(self, ring: HashRing, replication_factor: int = 2):
        self.ring = ring
        self.R = replication_factor
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def _get_owner_chain(self, key: str) -> list:
        """Return [primary, replica1, replica2, ...] for this key."""
        if not self.ring._ring:
            return []
        h = _hash(key)
        idx = bisect.bisect_right(self.ring._ring, (h, "")) % len(self.ring._ring)
        # Walk the ring to find R distinct nodes.
        chain = []
        seen = set()
        i = idx
        while len(chain) < self.R and len(seen) < len(self.ring._nodes):
            name = self.ring._ring[i % len(self.ring._ring)][1]
            if name not in seen:
                node = self.ring._nodes[name]
                if node.is_alive:
                    chain.append(node)
                seen.add(name)
            i += 1
        return chain

    def set(self, key: str, value: Any) -> None:
        chain = self._get_owner_chain(key)
        if not chain:
            raise RuntimeError("no alive nodes")
        primary = chain[0]
        primary.set(key, value)
        # Async replication to replicas (simulated synchronously here).
        for replica in chain[1:]:
            replica.replicate(key, value)

    def get(self, key: str) -> Optional[Any]:
        chain = self._get_owner_chain(key)
        if not chain:
            return None
        # Read from primary; fall back to replica if primary is down.
        for node in chain:
            val = node.get(key)
            if val is not None:
                return val
        return None

    def failover(self, dead_node_name: str) -> Optional[str]:
        """Promote the next replica for all keys owned by the dead node."""
        node = self.ring._nodes.get(dead_node_name)
        if node:
            node.kill()
        # The next get() on affected keys will find the next alive node
        # in the chain, effectively promoting it to primary.
        return f"Node {dead_node_name} killed; replicas auto-promoted"

# ---- Demo: cluster with 5 nodes, replication, failover ----
if __name__ == "__main__":
    ring = HashRing(vnodes=100)
    nodes = [CacheNode(f"node-{i}") for i in range(5)]
    for n in nodes:
        ring.add_node(n)

    cache = DistributedCache(ring, replication_factor=3)
    print(f"Cluster: {len(nodes)} nodes, R={cache.R}")

    # Write 1000 keys; verify primary placement and replication.
    for i in range(1000):
        cache.set(f"key-{i}", f"value-{i}")

    # Check replication: each key should be on primary + 2 replicas.
    sample_key = "key-42"
    chain = cache._get_owner_chain(sample_key)
    print(f"\nKey {sample_key} chain (primary -> replicas):")
    for i, node in enumerate(chain):
        role = "primary" if i == 0 else f"replica {i}"
        print(f"  {role}: {node.name} (value={node.get(sample_key)})")

    # Distribution: how many keys on each primary?
    primary_counts = {}
    for i in range(1000):
        node_name = ring.get_node_name(f"key-{i}")
        primary_counts[node_name] = primary_counts.get(node_name, 0) + 1
    print(f"\nPrimary distribution (should be ~balanced):")
    for name, count in sorted(primary_counts.items()):
        print(f"  {name}: {count} keys")

    # Failover: kill the primary of key-42, verify read still works.
    dead = chain[0].name
    print(f"\nKilling {dead} (primary of {sample_key})...")
    cache.failover(dead)
    val = cache.get(sample_key)
    print(f"Read after failover: {sample_key} = {val} (served from replica)")

    # Verify stats: replica got one extra read (from failover).
    print(f"\nStats for new primary ({chain[1].name}): {chain[1].stats}")
```
